Question: Describe the current responsibilities of all three teams, and explain the org changes that produced this structure, step by step.

**Current Responsibilities (as of today)** | Team | Core responsibilities | Typical deliverables | Primary stakeholders | |------|-----------------------|----------------------|----------------------| | **Frontend Team** | • Design, develop, and maintain all user‑facing UI components and experiences.
• Implement responsive layouts, accessibility, and performance optimizations for web (and, where applicable, mobile‑web) applications.
• Own the UI component library, design system, and front‑end build pipeline (webpack/ Vite, CI for UI).
• Work closely with product, UX, and QA to translate designs into production‑ready code.
• Conduct front‑end testing (unit, integration, visual regression) and support release validation. | • React/Vue/Angular (or other framework) codebases, component libraries, style guides, storybook docs.
• Front‑end CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configs, performance budgets.
• Feature toggles, A/B test harnesses, analytics instrumentation. | Product managers, UX designers, QA, Backend APIs, Platform (for CI/CD & hosting). | | **Backend Team** | • Design, implement, and maintain the core business‑logic services and public APIs (REST, GraphQL, gRPC, etc.).
• Own data‑modeling, domain services, transaction management, validation, and security (authz/authn) at the service layer.
• Provide SDKs, client libraries, and API documentation for internal & external consumers.
• Perform code reviews, unit/integration testing, and contract testing for services.
• Participate in incident response for business‑logic failures. | • Service codebases (micro‑services, monolith modules), API specifications (OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas).
• Database schema migrations, data‑access layers, background job workers.
• Service‑level monitoring dashboards, SLAs, and error‑budget tracking. | Frontend team (API consumers), Product, Data/Analytics, Platform (for deployment & observability). | | **Platform Team** | • Build, operate, and evolve the shared infrastructure that runs the Backend services and supports the Frontend pipelines.
• Provide cloud‑native foundations: Kubernetes clusters, CI/CD runners, IaC (Terraform/Pulumi), service mesh, observability stack (logging, tracing, metrics).
• Manage environments (dev, staging, prod), secrets management, networking, and security hardening.
• Offer self‑service platforms (PaaS, internal developer portals) for teams to deploy services, run jobs, and access common tooling.
• Automate reliability practices: automated roll‑backs, canary releases, chaos testing, capacity planning. | • Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Terraform modules, CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI).
• Centralized monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana), tracing (Jaeger/Zipkin), logging (ELK/EFK).
• Platform documentation, onboarding guides, internal SDKs for cloud services. | Backend team (runtime for services), Frontend team (CI/CD runners, static‑site hosting), Security, SRE/Operations. | --- ## How We Got Here – Step‑by‑Step Organizational Evolution Below is a chronological narrative that shows the key restructuring decisions and why each change was made. | Phase | Org shape | Reason for change | What moved where | |-------|-----------|-------------------|------------------| | **1️⃣ Initial State – Single “Full‑Stack” Team** | • One team handled both UI and server‑side code.
• Same engineers wrote React components *and* the Java/Spring (or Node) services that powered them.
• Infrastructure was managed ad‑hoc by the same group (e.g., manual VM provisioning). | • Early product was small; a single team could ship end‑to‑end features quickly.
• Overhead of coordination was low, and the codebase was tightly coupled. | All responsibilities (frontend, backend, infrastructure) lived in one “Full‑Stack” squad. | | **2️⃣ First Split – Dedicated Frontend & Backend Teams** | • Two distinct squads: **Frontend** (UI/UX focus) and **Backend** (business logic & APIs).
• Infrastructure still handled by the Backend group as a “side‑task”. | • Product grew; UI complexity demanded specialized skill sets (design systems, performance tuning).
• Backend services became more numerous and required deeper domain expertise, testing, and versioning. | • Frontend team took ownership of all client‑side code, design system, and UI pipelines.
• Backend team inherited all server‑side services, data models, and the “infrastructure” chores that were previously done manually. | | **3️⃣ Second Split – Carving Out a Platform Team** | • Three squads: **Frontend**, **Backend**, **Platform**.
• Platform was a subset of the former Backend team, focusing exclusively on infrastructure. | • The Backend engineers were spending an increasing amount of time on ops‑related tasks (Kubernetes, CI/CD, monitoring) that distracted them from core business logic.
• Scaling the system required a more systematic, repeatable infrastructure approach (IaC, self‑service deployment). | • **Platform team** took over all cloud‑native infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, observability, security hardening, and environment management.
• **Backend team** retained only the domain‑level services, API contracts, and data‑layer responsibilities. | | **4️⃣ Stabilization – Current Structure** | • **Frontend** continues to own the UI stack (unchanged since the first split).
• **Backend** now focuses *solely* on business logic, APIs, and data‑access – no longer responsible for provisioning servers, clusters, or CI/CD runners.
• **Platform** provides the “runtime” and tooling that both Frontend and Backend consume. | • Clear separation of concerns improves focus, reduces context‑switching, and enables each team to hire and grow expertise in its domain.
• Platform can standardize deployments, enforce security policies, and drive reliability improvements across the entire product line.
• Frontend can iterate quickly on UI without worrying about infra; Backend can evolve APIs without being blocked by infra changes. | No further moves; the three‑team model is now the stable operating model. | ### Summary of the Evolution 1. **Full‑Stack Team → Two Teams** – Growth of product complexity made it worthwhile to specialize. UI work and server work diverged in skill set and tooling, prompting the first split. 2. **Two Teams → Three Teams** – As the backend services scaled, the “ops” workload (cloud provisioning, CI/CD, monitoring) grew to a size that warranted a dedicated group. The Platform team was formed to own that workload, freeing the Backend team to focus on the *what* (business logic) rather than the *how* (infrastructure). 3. **Current State** – The three teams now have clean, non‑overlapping responsibility boundaries: * **Frontend** → *What the user sees and interacts with.* * **Backend** → *What the system does (business rules, data handling, APIs).* * **Platform** → *Where the system runs and how it’s delivered (infrastructure, CI/CD, observability).* This step‑by‑step re‑organization has allowed the organization to scale both the product and the engineering workforce while maintaining high velocity, reliability, and clear ownership.
